title: Water security in the metropolitan region of Rio de Janeiro: contributions to the debate
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic — water-resource study unrelated to household or community service access, Exclusion Criterion 7). The article examines bulk raw-water resource security and river-basin governance in the Metropolitan Region of Rio de Janeiro, focusing on inter-state disputes over Paraíba do Sul river transposition, Rio de Janeiro's water-resources management statutes and instruments (basin plans, raw-water abstraction grants, bulk water-use charges), the Guandu River Basin Committee, and landfill leachate threats to the Piranema Aquifer. It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access or rule-type mechanisms governing service access, and relies on a narrative review of literature, statutes, state technical reports, and the author's prior dissertation rather than primary empirical access data. Even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because it fails Criteria 1, 3, 4, and 5.

title: Systems thinking approach for analysing non-revenue water management reform in Malaysia
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome; also fails c1 service access). While this qualitative systems-thinking study empirically examines Malaysian water utility regulatory, ownership, licensing, and tariff-setting reforms (WSIA 2006 and SPAN Act 2006), it investigates their effects solely on utility-level Non-Revenue Water (NRW) reduction and leakage management rather than household or community water service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. Under both the active narrow rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study is excluded for lacking a household/community service-access focus and outcome.

title: Water, sanitation, and women’s empowerment: A systematic review and qualitative metasynthesis
rationale: This PRISMA systematic review and qualitative metasynthesis synthesizes 257 empirical studies on water, sanitation, and women's and girls' empowerment. While it satisfies c1 (water and sanitation access), c3 (systematic empirical synthesis), c4 (reports latrine ownership, water access/quantity, affordability trade-offs, and exclusion alongside empowerment outcomes), c5, and c6, it fails Criterion 2 under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism scope (exclude: E03, wrong exposure). Its conceptual framework maps general empowerment domains (94% Resources such as violence, health, privacy, time, and household assets; Agency; and informal gender norms and relations). The small 'Formal Laws & Policies' sub-domain (21 of 257 studies) primarily addresses gender quotas and representation on community WASH committees, female entrepreneurship, watershed projects, or brief unanalysed mentions of school/camp guidelines rather than analysing a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community service access. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because it explicitly synthesizes institutional structures, formal policies, and community WASH governance alongside service access outcomes.

title: Human right to sanitation in the legal and non-legal literature: the need for greater synergy
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Obani and Gupta (2016) present a narrative, conceptual, and doctrinal overview comparing how legal and non-legal scholars frame the human right to sanitation (HRS) and human right to water and sanitation (HRWS). Although the paper discusses sanitation access (c1) and legal/regulatory mechanisms such as tariffs, cost recovery, tenure security, and accountability (c2 under both plain and narrow readings), it collects no primary data and does not conduct a systematic empirical synthesis with defined eligibility criteria, study selection counts, or extracted empirical access outcomes (failing c3, c4, and c5).

title: Watershed protection challenges in rapidly Urbanizing regions: The case of tegucigalpa, honduras
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; see Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). The paper focuses on upstream watershed and source-water protection in the Guacerique catchment and Los Laureles reservoir supplying Tegucigalpa, Honduras—specifically land-use encroachment, non-enforcement of forestry/zoning laws, reservoir siltation, raw water contamination, and cuts to SANAA's watershed management budget—explicitly contrasting neglected watershed protection with downstream consumer coverage expansion. In addition, it is a non-empirical narrative policy overview relying on secondary reports with no primary data or identifiable empirical study design (failing c1, c2 under the narrow rule-type reading, c3, c4, and c5).

title: Cost Efficiency, Urban Patterns and Population Density When Providing Public Infrastructure: A Stochastic Frontier Approach
rationale: Excluded (E01 - Wrong topic; also fails C2 and C4). This regional/urban economics paper estimates a translog stochastic cost frontier for the physical capital stock of municipal water and wastewater infrastructure across 999 municipalities in Castilla y León, Spain, to quantify economies of scale, spatial density economies, and cost-minimizing population density. It explicitly studies municipal infrastructure construction/replacement cost efficiency as a function of settlement dispersion and demographic scale rather than household or community water/sanitation service access (failing C1 and C4), and it does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance factor under either the plain wording or the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (failing C2).

title: PROJECT FINANCING STRATEGIES AND PERFORMANCE OF WATER SUPPLY PROJECTS IN NYANZA REGION, KENYA
rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure), alongside lacking a household/community service-access outcome (c1/c4). This mixed-methods survey of 457 project stakeholders in Nyanza Region, Kenya examines how infrastructure project financing strategies (internal funds, debt, equity, mezzanine, donor grants) predict generic stakeholder-perceived 'Performance of Water Supply Projects'. Although water policy is mentioned in the theoretical framing, it is never empirically analysed (as acknowledged on p. 12), so the study tests generic project capital financing rather than a legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance rule-type mechanism governing water access, and reports no household or community access, connection, reliability, availability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome. Both narrow and plain Criterion 2 readings result in exclusion.

title: Insights into water insecurity in Indigenous communities in Canada: assessing microbial risks and innovative solutions, a multifaceted review
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). The article is a non-systematic narrative 'multifaceted review' ('This is a literature review') synthesizing secondary literature and government portals on microbial risks in water storage tanks, natural organic matter (NOM), drinking water treatment processes and molecular microbial monitoring tools (metagenomics, culturomics and microfluidics). In addition to lacking primary empirical governance-access analysis or systematic-review methodology (c3 = no, c5 = no), the authors explicitly restrict their scope to technical and microbiological issues, treating shared federal/First Nations governance and regulatory fragmentation only as unanalysed background (c2 = no under narrow rule-type scope; plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude).

title: Water security: stakeholders’ arena in the Awash River Basin of Ethiopia
rationale: Excluded (E01 - Wrong topic; per Exclusion Criterion 7, water-resource study unrelated to household or community service access). Although empirical (29 KIIs and 16 FGDs), this paper is a river-basin-scale Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) stakeholder analysis examining inter-agency coordination, power asymmetries, irrigation canal maintenance, upstream agricultural abstractions, and industrial effluent pollution in the Awash River Basin rather than household or community water supply or sanitation service access (failing C1). It also fails C2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type reading because it examines macro/basin-level resource governance and environmental pollution enforcement rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household/community service access, and fails C4 because its empirical outcomes are stakeholder influence-interest matrices and expert Likert ratings of general basin water-resource challenges rather than household/community service-access outcomes. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded due to failing C1 and C4.

title: Building Rain Water Tanks and Building Skills: A Case Study of a Women's Organization in Uganda
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). This empirical case study evaluates an NGO vocational training program that trained 22 rural Ugandan women as ferro-cement rainwater tank masons, focusing on the masons' income gains, empowerment, and gender/logistical challenges in the masonry trade. It does not examine a legal, administrative, regulatory, or rule-type governance mechanism governing household water access (a brief three-sentence description of a 10%-deposit tank revolving loan scheme on p. 180 is unanalysed project background rather than an empirically studied exposure).

title: Flows of change: dynamic water rights and water access in peri-urban Kathmandu
rationale: Full-text ethnographic socio-legal study in peri-urban Kathmandu Valley, Nepal, meeting all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2. Although the Dadhikot case focuses mainly on agricultural irrigation canals, the Jhaukhel case directly investigates household drinking/domestic water access and commercial urban water supply, showing how land-tenure-based groundwater claims, overlapping business vs. water-board registration/permitting rules, and explicit regulatory discretion and non-enforcement of the 2012 Groundwater Policy by KVWSMB and the VDC lead to depletion of household wells/spouts, exclusion of women seeking drinking water, and household dependence on commercial water factories and vendors. Qualitative socio-legal studies with identifiable empirical methods are eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis.

title: The challenge of integration in the implementation of Zimbabwe's new water policy: Case study of the catchment level institutions surrounding the Pungwe-Mutare water supply project

Using interviews, meeting observations, and council records in Zimbabwe's Save Catchment Area, Tapela (2002) examines institutional challenges facing the Save Catchment Council and Pungwe Sub-Catchment Council—inter-agency coordination, stakeholder and gender representation on councils, commercial farmer dominance, and conflict resolution over commercial/irrigation raw-water permits. rationale: Full text matches metadata (Saadi & Johns 2026, Water Policy, DOI 10.2166/wp.2026.214). Excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence). It collects no primary empirical data and is not a reproducible systematic empirical synthesis (search, deduplication, screening, and exclusion counts were not preserved, and municipal strategy documents are summarized descriptively to develop an unvalidated cyclical policy framework). In addition, it focuses on utility digital technology governance and operational resilience rather than household/community service access (failing c1), examines macro/organizational smart-water implementation conditions rather than a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism governing access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification (passing plain c2 wording but failing narrow c2), and reports no empirical service-access outcomes (failing c4 and c5). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded due to lack of primary empirical evidence or systematic empirical synthesis of access outcomes.

title: A Concrete Response to Poverty? Rethinking Approaches to Urban Poverty and Infrastructure: A Zambian Case Study
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Cottam (1997) is a Foucauldian theoretical and policy essay in IDS Bulletin critiquing orthodox urban poverty and 'Fordist' infrastructure discourse, illustrated with a brief prospective overview of the low-income component of the World Bank-funded Zambia Urban Restructuring and Water Supply Project. As Footnote 3 notes, the project description is drawn from an outline in World Bank (1994), the project was only in the initial stages of implementation (with financial investment expected up to a year after start-up), and the article reports no empirical methods, primary data, sample, or measured access outcomes. In addition, under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, the paper focuses on macro-development discourse and participatory project delivery rather than examining a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism governing service access; even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded for lack of empirical evidence (E05).

title: Environmental and socio-economic determinants of fecal sludge emptying in Sub-Saharan Africa: A cross-sectional mixed-methods study in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire
rationale: This cross-sectional mixed-methods study in Yopougon, Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Quantitatively, it estimates the association between household tenure (homeownership vs. tenancy, aOR = 0.27 for unsafe vs. safe mechanical emptying) and uptake of formal mechanical fecal sludge emptying services among 359 households, linking tenure disparities to statutory landlord obligations under the Construction and Housing Code. Qualitatively, through 24 stakeholder interviews analyzed via thematic content analysis, it directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing service access and affordability: lack of tariff regulation for private emptying trucks coupled with a sanitation tax deducted on water bills, and non-enforcement of national Water Code provisions and municipal fines due to unfunded decentralization.

Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, it remains excluded due to failing C1 and C4.

It contains no empirical methodology, no primary data collection design (aside from one brief uncontextualised quote from an unpublished 2007 CD), and no systematic synthesis protocol, relying instead on descriptive summary tables compiled from UN-HABITAT, World Bank (Keener et al.), Gleick et al., and IBNET reports. It also fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because it examines macro-level capital investment shortfalls, demographic pressure, and broad private-sector investment avoidance rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household water access. title: Environmental injustice and human rights violations in Jalisco, Mexico; [Injusticia ambiental y violaciones de los derechos humanos en Jalisco, México]
rationale: Exclude under E01 (Wrong topic). This qualitative documentary study analyzes 35 recommendations issued by the Jalisco State Human Rights Commission (CEDHJ) from 2000 to 2022 concerning violations of the constitutional right to a healthy environment (derecho al ambiente sano) across environmental injustice themes (surface-water pollution, biodiversity loss, solid waste landfills, soil pesticide contamination, noise, and air pollution), detailing three cases of industrial river pollution, landfill mismanagement, and agrochemical exposure. It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1=no), does not analyze a rule-type mechanism governing water or sanitation service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification (c2=no, though it passes the plain governance wording of c2), and reports no water or sanitation service access outcomes (c4=no).

title: Creating a Decentralized Integrated Performance Index Water Supply System: An Examination of SiPAS in the Brantas River Basin
rationale: Excluded at full text (E03: Wrong exposure; also fails Criterion 4 on outcome). This water-resources engineering study constructs and calibrates a composite site-level Performance Index Model (IKSiPAS = 0.7833 IKTechnical + 0.1011 IKSocial + 0.1156 IKManagement) across 31 community-managed rural water supply systems (SiPAS) in Indonesia using SEM-PLS and GRG optimization, and deploys an Android mobile app for real-time maintenance work orders. Under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, it does not examine any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access—its managerial construct captures generic organizational/operator capacity (institutional capacity, financial planning, human resources, generic governance quality/regulatory compliance), and its intervention is a digital maintenance tool. Moreover, even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study would still be excluded because IKManagement is an additive sub-component of the composite performance score IKSiPAS itself rather than an exposure tested against a disaggregated water access, connection, continuity, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome, and the app evaluation measures only repair cycle time, work-order closure rate, non-revenue-water loss, and ΔIKTechnical.

title: Workplace menstrual health in the private sector: Results from a pilot study in Kenya and Nepal
rationale: Excluded (E01 - Wrong topic). This study evaluates a USAID WASHPaLS private-sector workplace menstrual health (MH) pilot program across four manufacturing factories in Kenya and Nepal aimed at improving menstrual management on the job, women's economic empowerment, and business outcomes. It fails Criterion 1 because it studies private-sector workplace menstrual health management (menstrual pad/cup provision, MHH education, menstrual stigma/leave, and factory washroom upgrades) rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. It also fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 clarification because it evaluates a bundled NGO project-delivery and behavioural-promotion intervention (free products, BCC/Appreciative Inquiry, toilet repairs, and general internal HR policy recommendations) rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access, and fails Criterion 4 because its measured outcomes concern menstrual knowledge, pad comfort/supply, workplace support/leave, absenteeism, work performance, and job satisfaction (with facility items dropped from the endline survey). Even under the plain broad reading of Criterion 2, the paper remains excluded on Criteria 1 and 4.
